en: Wealthy; having a lot of money
hook: AFFLUENT: money FLOWS in (fluent).
story: Affluent. Wealthy; having plenty of money. Every winter, Lamia's family took the bus from Mirpur to visit her mother's cousin in Gulshan. The gate opened onto a green lawn and a dining table so long that Lamia counted the chairs twice. Her cousin was kind, but Lamia suddenly felt shy in her old school shoes. It was her first close look at an affluent home. Affluent comes from the Latin for flowing toward, the same root as fluent: in an affluent family, money simply flows in. So, what word describes a family with plenty of money? ... Affluent.

gre.s: Although the town was once ____, sustained by a booming textile trade, it sank into poverty when the mills closed and its young people moved away.
gre.clue: sustained by a booming textile trade

example: As the suburb grew more affluent, its small tailoring shops gave way to boutiques selling imported clothes.

en: Covering every part or aspect, leaving nothing out
hook: ALL-ENCOMPASSING: a COMPASS that circles everything.
story: All-encompassing. Covering every part, leaving nothing out. In the last month before Nadia's HSC exams, her preparation took over the whole house. Formula charts were taped to the kitchen wall, her younger brother quizzed her at breakfast, and her father stopped watching the evening news so the flat stayed quiet. Nobody in the family escaped it. The exam had become all-encompassing. To encompass is to draw a circle around something, like the circle a compass makes, so an all-encompassing thing holds everything inside its circle. So, what word describes something that takes in every part, leaving nothing out? ... All-encompassing.

gre.s: Far from the narrow survey its modest title suggested, the study was nearly ____, covering every aspect of the region's economy from river fishing to software.
gre.clue: covering every aspect of the region's economy

example: Her grief after the accident was all-encompassing, colouring every meal, every conversation and every song she heard on the radio.

en: Similar or comparable in some way
hook: ANALOGOUS: makes an ANALOGY possible.
story: Analogous. Similar or comparable in some way. The class nine biology students in Khulna were lost in diagrams of the heart. Then their teacher, Kamal Sir, pointed out of the window at the tube well in the school yard. "The heart pushes blood the way that pump pushes water, and its valves stop the flow from running back." One by one, the faces lit up. The heart is analogous to a pump. Analogous and analogy share a Greek root: analogous things are alike enough to make an analogy. So, what word describes two things similar enough to compare? ... Analogous.

gre.s: The author argues that the decline of the empire is ____ to the collapse of a modern corporation, since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry.
gre.clue: since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry

example: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are analogous structures, since both allow flight but they evolved entirely separately.

en: Very old or old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use
hook: ARCHAIC: as old as ARCHAEOLOGY digs.
story: Archaic. Very old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use. In a tin trunk at her grandmother's house in Barishal, Joya found a bundle of letters from the nineteen sixties, written in sadhu bhasha, the formal old Bangla. She read one aloud, [chuckle] stumbling over the grand, stiff verbs, and her grandmother [laugh] clapped her hands. "That is how we wrote then!" To Joya the language sounded archaic, yet she loved every line. Archaic shares a Greek root with archaeology, the study of ancient things: archaic words belong to an older world. So, what word describes language no longer in everyday use? ... Archaic.

gre.s: Although the statute remains on the books, it is so ____ that no court has enforced it in over a century.
gre.clue: no court has enforced it in over a century

example: Several archaic words, such as thou and hath, survive in the old hymns the choir still sings each Christmas.

en: Excessively complicated and involving many confusing details, especially bureaucracy
hook: BYZANTINE: like the ancient Byzantine Empire's maze-like bureaucracy.
story: Byzantine. Excessively complicated and confusing, especially rules and paperwork. To register his small tailoring shop, Kamal needed a form from one office, a stamp from another, and a signature from an officer who was never at his desk. Each clerk sent him to a different floor. After three months in hot corridors, [sigh] he was holding the same form he started with. The process was byzantine. The word recalls the Byzantine Empire, whose court became famous for its maze of officials and rules. So, what word describes paperwork so tangled that nobody can find a way through? ... Byzantine.

gre.s: The tax code has become so ____ that even professional accountants struggle to navigate its thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions.
gre.clue: thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions

example: Getting a refund from the airline involved a byzantine process of forms, phone calls and emails that dragged on for nearly six months.

en: To examine and remove objectionable parts from media
hook: CENSOR: CUTS out what's forbidden. Not censure (criticize).
story: Censor. To examine books, films or news and remove the parts considered unacceptable. Ishita's grandfather edited a newspaper during a time of strict government control. Every night, officials read his pages and cut out any line they disliked. Some mornings the paper appeared with blank white columns, and readers understood exactly what had been censored. The officials were called censors, a title borrowed from ancient Roman officers who judged public behaviour. Do not confuse it with censure, which means to criticise harshly. So, what verb means to cut parts from the news before anyone reads them? ... Censor.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the novel's explicit passages, as the publisher had demanded, the author withdrew the manuscript entirely, insisting that every word remain intact.
gre.clue: insisting that every word remain intact

example: Wartime officials censored soldiers' letters home, blacking out any mention of where the troops were stationed.

en: Standing out clearly; easy to notice
hook: CON-SPIC-uous: SPIC sounds like 'spec', as in spectacle. Everyone can see it.
story: Conspicuous. Standing out clearly; easy to notice. At his cousin's wedding in Chattogram, everyone wore soft pastel colours. Then Arif walked in wearing the bright orange panjabi his mother had chosen. Heads turned and aunties whispered. Arif felt his ears grow hot, but his little niece ran over, [laugh] and said he looked like a marigold. He was the most conspicuous man in the hall. The spic inside conspicuous comes from the Latin for look, as in spectacle: a conspicuous thing makes everyone look. So, what word describes something impossible to miss? ... Conspicuous.

gre.s: The detective was puzzled that the thief had chosen such a ____ getaway car, a bright yellow convertible that half the town would remember.
gre.clue: half the town would remember

example: As the only tall tree among the paddy fields, the old palm is conspicuous from miles away and guides travelers to the village.

en: Familiar with and at ease in many different countries and cultures
hook: COSMOS = world, POLIS = city. A citizen of the world.
story: Cosmopolitan. At ease in many countries and cultures. Mitu's aunt has worked as a nurse in London, Nairobi and Toronto. At a family dinner in Dhanmondi, she chatted with a visiting Japanese engineer, switched to Bangla to tease her nephews, then explained a Kenyan bean stew to Mitu's grandmother. She seemed at home with everyone. Mitu decided she wanted to be that cosmopolitan one day. The word joins the Greek kosmos, world, and polites, citizen, so a cosmopolitan person is a citizen of the world. So, what word describes someone comfortable in many cultures? ... Cosmopolitan.

gre.s: The port's ____ character, shaped by centuries of traders from dozens of nations, contrasted sharply with the insular villages of the interior.
gre.clue: contrasted sharply with the insular villages

example: Chattogram has long been a cosmopolitan port, where Arab, Portuguese and Burmese traders once mingled along the banks of the Karnaphuli.

en: A mistaken belief that someone clings to in spite of clear proof
hook: DELUSION: an ILLUSION you won't let go of.
story: Delusion. A false belief someone clings to despite clear proof. Tareq skipped every mock test, yet he told his friends he would score near the top of the GRE because he was naturally sharp. When his practice scores came back low, he blamed the website. Finally his friend Sara said gently, "Tareq, the scores are real. Let's study together." Slowly, the delusion cracked. An illusion fools your eyes; a delusion fools your mind, and you refuse to let it go. So, what word means a false belief held on to against all evidence? ... Delusion.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt, the founder clung to the ____ that a single blockbuster product would restore its fortunes.
gre.clue: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt

example: Many smokers cling to the delusion that they can quit whenever they like, long after the habit has taken hold.

en: A follower of a teacher, leader, or philosophy
hook: DISCIPLE: follows the DISCIPLINE of a master.
story: Disciple. A follower of a teacher, leader or way of thinking. Every evening, in an old house in Kushtia, a group of young singers sat on the floor learning Lalon songs from an elderly master. They copied his breath, his gestures, even the way he closed his eyes. Years later, one of them became famous, and in every interview he called himself a humble disciple of that master. Disciple and discipline come from the same Latin root for learning: a disciple accepts a teacher's discipline. So, what word means a devoted follower of a teacher? ... Disciple.

gre.s: Far from rejecting his mentor's theories, the young economist proved to be her most faithful ____, defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them.
gre.clue: defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them

example: As a young disciple of the sitar master, Nazmul spent years practising scales before he was allowed to perform in public.

en: Spreading apart; different from each other
hook: DI-VERGE: two paths going different ways.
story: Divergent. Moving apart in different directions; different from each other. Twin sisters Priya and Puja shared one room, one bicycle and one cricket bat until they were eighteen. Then their paths split. Priya went to study medicine in Dhaka, while Puja stayed in Sylhet, took over their father's tea stall and later opened her own small restaurant. Their lives became divergent, yet every night they still talked on the phone. To diverge is to split away, like a road forking in two; its opposite, converge, means to come together. So, what word describes paths that move apart? ... Divergent.

gre.s: The two economists' forecasts are sharply ____, one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession.
gre.clue: one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession

example: Raised in the same house, the two cousins held sharply divergent views on almost every political question of the day.

en: Picking freely from many different sources or styles
hook: ECLECTIC: ELECTS a bit from everywhere.
story: Eclectic. Choosing freely from many different sources or styles. Joya's hostel room surprises every visitor. A Rabindra Sangeet record sits beside a Korean pop poster, a baul's ektara hangs above a shelf of Japanese comics, and her bedspread is a nakshi kantha her grandmother stitched. Her friends [chuckle] call it a museum. Joya simply says she keeps whatever she loves. Her taste is eclectic. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to pick out, so think of select: an eclectic person selects the best from everywhere. So, what word describes taste drawn from many different styles? ... Eclectic.

gre.s: The architect's style resists easy categorization: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction, it is thoroughly ____.
gre.clue: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction

example: Nilufar's bookshelf is wonderfully eclectic, holding Bengali folk tales, Russian novels, cookbooks and a manual for repairing motorbikes.

en: Native to or regularly found in a particular place or group
hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
story: Endemic. Regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group. Every monsoon, as rainwater gathers in flowerpots and old tyres, dengue returns to Dhaka. Doctors are no longer surprised; hospitals prepare beds before the rains even begin. Dengue is endemic in Bangladesh, always present, rising and falling with the seasons. The word can also describe plants or animals native to one place. Endemic joins en, meaning in, and demos, meaning people: it lives in the people. Its cousin epidemic is a sudden outbreak. So, what word describes a disease that is always present in one region? ... Endemic.

gre.s: Corruption was so ____ in the old regime that bribery was considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal.
gre.clue: considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal

example: Cheating was endemic at the exam centre, so the board sent outside invigilators and installed cameras in every hall.

en: Fair and impartial
hook: EQUITABLE: EQUAL for all.
story: Equitable. Fair and impartial. When their father decided to retire and divide his mango orchard in Rajshahi, three brothers feared a quarrel. Their father walked the whole orchard, counted every tree, and drew the lines so that each son got the same number of fruiting trees and an equal path to the pond. The youngest brother [sigh] smiled with relief. Everyone agreed the division was equitable. Equitable shares its root with equal and equity: an equitable split is equal for all. So, what word describes a division that is fair to everyone? ... Equitable.

gre.s: Critics argued that the new tax was hardly ____, since it fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched.
gre.clue: fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched

example: The roommates worked out an equitable rota for washing dishes, based on how often each of them actually cooked.

en: To grow quickly worse, bigger or more serious
hook: ESCALATE: like an ESCALATOR, going up and up.
story: Escalate. To grow quickly bigger, worse or more serious. It began when a rickshaw brushed a motorbike's mirror in a narrow lane of Old Dhaka. The rider shouted, the rickshaw puller shouted back, and soon shopkeepers were taking sides. Within ten minutes a crowd blocked the lane. Then an old tea seller stepped in with two cups of tea and calmed everyone before it could escalate further. The word escalate was formed from escalator: picture a moving staircase carrying a quarrel up and up. So, what verb means to grow quickly more serious? ... Escalate.

gre.s: What began as a minor quarrel over a parking space threatened to ____ into a brawl as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides.
gre.clue: as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides

example: Prices at the cattle markets escalated sharply in the final days before Eid, as buyers rushed to find animals.

en: Perfectly clean and tidy; flawless
hook: IM-MACULATE: without a single spot (macula).
story: Immaculate. Perfectly clean and tidy; flawless. The night before the hostel inspection, Ishita scrubbed her floor twice, folded every kameez, lined up her books by height, and wiped the window bars with a damp cloth. In the morning, the strict warden ran one finger along the shelf, looked at it, and found nothing. "Immaculate," she said, and for the first time she smiled. Ishita [sigh] sank onto her bed. In Latin, macula means a spot or stain, so immaculate means without a single spot. So, what word describes a room so clean you cannot find a speck of dust? ... Immaculate.

gre.s: Though the pianist had been ill all week, her performance was ____: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none.
gre.clue: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none

example: Even after a twelve-hour flight, the captain's white uniform looked immaculate as he walked through the terminal.

en: Cleverly inventive, especially in finding new ways to solve problems
hook: INGENIOUS: a GENIUS idea. Not to be confused with ingenuous (innocent).
story: Ingenious. Cleverly inventive, especially at solving problems. In the wetlands of Pirojpur, fields stay underwater for months each year. Long ago, farmers there found an answer. They piled water hyacinth into thick floating rafts, topped them with mud, and grew vegetables that rose and fell with the water. On a field trip, Mahin watched an old farmer pull fresh okra from a raft and felt a quiet pride. The floating gardens were ingenious. Ingenious shares a Latin root with engine, meaning natural talent; do not confuse it with ingenuous, innocent. So, what word describes a clever, inventive solution? ... Ingenious.

gre.s: The engineer's ____ design, which used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump, succeeded where expensive imported machines had repeatedly failed.
gre.clue: used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump

example: The ingenious puzzle box has no visible lock and opens only when its wooden panels are slid in a precise order.

en: A secret plot or scheme; to arouse curiosity
hook: INTRIGUE: the palace's secret plots that INTRIGUE you.
story: Intrigue. A secret plot or scheme; as a verb, to make someone curious. Lamia found a historical novel about Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah on her uncle's shelf. In its pages, courtiers whispered in dark corridors and plotted with foreign traders to bring their ruler down. The palace intrigue intrigued her so deeply that she read until two in the morning, [gasp] catching her breath at every betrayal. Intrigue shares its root with intricate: both come from the Latin for tangled, and a plot is a tangle of secrets. So, what word names a secret plot, and also the curiosity it stirs? ... Intrigue.

gre.s: The royal court was rife with ____: ministers formed secret alliances, spread rumors about their rivals, and plotted against one another behind the king's back.
gre.clue: plotted against one another behind the king's back

example: The novel follows a young clerk caught up in the intrigue of a family firm, where cousins secretly plot to seize control.

en: Letting no light through; also, difficult to make sense of
hook: OPAQUE: light can't pass through; meaning can't pass through either.
story: Opaque. Letting no light through; also, hard to understand. The bathroom window in Shuvo's flat is frosted glass: light comes in, but no one can see through it. That same afternoon, his economics professor spent an hour on monetary policy, filling the board with symbols and never stopping for questions. Shuvo looked down at his notes and [sigh] saw nothing but fog. The lecture was as opaque as his window. Opaque is the opposite of transparent: when meaning cannot pass through, an explanation is opaque. So, what word describes writing or speech you simply cannot see into? ... Opaque.

gre.s: Critics complained that the company's accounting was deliberately ____, making it nearly impossible for investors to understand where the money went.
gre.clue: nearly impossible for investors to understand

example: The ministry's scholarship selection process remained opaque, and no applicant was ever told why they had been rejected.

en: Closely connected to the subject being discussed
hook: PERTINENT: PERTAINS to the topic.
story: Pertinent. Closely connected to the subject being discussed. In his first job interview at a shipping company in Chattogram, Rafi was asked how he handled pressure. Instead, he described one night during his internship when a shipment was delayed and he called the port every hour until it moved. The panel leaned forward and nodded. His answer was short and pertinent. Pertinent sounds like pertain, and they share a root: a pertinent point pertains to the topic. So, what word describes a remark directly relevant to the matter at hand? ... Pertinent.

gre.s: The judge excluded the testimony as not ____ to the case, since it concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime.
gre.clue: concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime

example: Before the vote, the councillor raised a pertinent question about who would pay to maintain the new park once it was built.

en: Present in every part of a place or group
hook: PERVASIVE: PERVADES everything, like a smell filling a house.
story: Pervasive. Spreading through every part of a place or group. On the first morning of the Eid holidays, Farhan's mother fried onions for the biryani. Within minutes the rich smell had spread into every room, every curtain and every pillow. Two days later, Farhan opened his cupboard, and [laugh] even his shirts smelled of onions. The smell was pervasive. Pervasive comes from pervade, from the Latin per, through, and vadere, to go: a pervasive thing goes through everything. So, what word describes something that has spread into every corner? ... Pervasive.

gre.s: Researchers found the influence of social media so ____ that it shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives.
gre.clue: shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives

example: Fear of failure was so pervasive at the coaching centre that students hid their practice scores even from close friends.

en: To recommend a medicine; to state authoritatively what should be done
hook: PRE-SCRIBE: write (scribe) the rule BEFORE.
story: Prescribe. To recommend a medicine; also, to state with authority what must be done. Tania went to a clinic in Rangpur with a fever. The doctor listened to her chest, then wrote on a slip of paper: one tablet three times a day and complete rest for five days. He had prescribed both medicine and rules, and Tania, who hated sitting still, reluctantly obeyed. Prescribe comes from the Latin for write before: the doctor writes down what must happen. Do not confuse it with proscribe, which means to forbid. So, what verb means to order a remedy? ... Prescribe.

gre.s: Unlike earlier grammarians, who sought to ____ rigid rules for correct usage, modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak.
gre.clue: modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak

example: School rules prescribe a white shirt and navy trousers, but many pupils add bright socks as a small act of rebellion.

en: To feel bitterness about unfair treatment
hook: RE-SENT: the insult is SENT back again and again in your mind.
story: Resent. To feel bitter about unfair treatment. For years, Imran's younger brother got the new clothes, the bigger room and all the praise, while Imran carried the shopping and fixed the ceiling fan. He never complained aloud, but he resented every small unfairness. Then one Eid, his brother quietly handed him the first new panjabi and said, "Your turn, bhaiya." Imran felt the old resentment loosen. Resent comes from the French re, again, and sentir, to feel: to resent is to feel a hurt again and again. So, what verb means to feel bitter at being treated unfairly? ... Resent.

gre.s: Veteran staff members tended to ____ the newcomers' rapid promotions, which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit.
gre.clue: which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit

example: Local fishermen resent the new trawlers from the city, which sweep up in one night what a small boat catches in a month.

en: Using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize people's foolishness
hook: SATIRICAL: SATIRE makes fun of the powerful.
story: Satirical. Using humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise foolishness. Every week, Kamal waits for the cartoon page of his newspaper. This week it showed a minister cutting the ribbon on a new bridge while the bridge itself floated away in the flood behind him. Kamal [chuckle] showed it to his father, and both laughed, then fell quiet. The joke had a sharp point about wasted money. The cartoon was satirical. Satire smiles, but it bites: its laughter always carries a criticism. So, what word describes humour used to expose foolishness or wrongdoing? ... Satirical.

gre.s: The magazine's ____ cartoons, which exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths, made him a laughingstock across the country.
gre.clue: exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths

example: Swift's satirical essay proposed that the poor of Ireland sell their babies as food, a shocking idea meant to expose official cruelty.

en: Thinly scattered; small in number or amount
hook: SPARSE: SPARE, very little.
story: Sparse. Thinly scattered; small in number or amount. One winter, Anika's family drove north toward Panchagarh. Near Dhaka the roads were packed with shops and people, but by evening the villages grew sparse: a few tin roofs, a lone tea stall, wide fields of yellow mustard under fog. Anika rolled down her window and breathed the cold, quiet air. Even the street lights were sparse. Sparse comes from the Latin for scattered, like seeds tossed loosely across a field. Its opposite is dense. So, what word describes things thinly scattered across a wide space? ... Sparse.

gre.s: Attendance at the lecture was ____: barely a dozen listeners sat dotted across an auditorium built to hold five hundred.
gre.clue: barely a dozen listeners

example: Data on the rare river dolphins of the Sangu is sparse, so researchers rely partly on reports from local fishermen.

en: Showing simplicity and a lack of luxury; austere
hook: SPARTAN: like the warriors of SPARTA, tough and simple.
story: Spartan. Simple and plain, with no comfort or luxury. When Zayan joined a cadet college, his room held a narrow iron bed, a thin mattress, one table and a steel trunk. Wake-up was at five, the water was cold, and lights went out at ten. At first, he wrote home every night. By the end of the year, he was proud of how little he needed. Life there was spartan. The ancient Spartans of Greece were famous for their tough, simple way of life. So, what word describes a plain lifestyle with no luxuries at all? ... Spartan.

gre.s: The monks' ____ quarters contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle.
gre.clue: contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle

example: Mountaineers on the expedition lived a spartan life, melting snow for water and sleeping in thin tents at minus thirty.

en: Quiet and reflective, often slightly sad; soft and restrained
hook: SUBDUED: SUBjugated, toned down.
story: Subdued. Quiet and restrained, often a little sad; also soft and toned down. Babu was usually the loudest boy in the hostel, telling stories at every meal. But in the week after his grandmother passed away, he ate slowly, answered in single words, and spent his evenings by the window. They understood why he was so subdued. The word also describes soft, gentle light, like the subdued lamps of a library. To subdue is to bring under control, so a subdued person holds their feelings down. So, what word describes someone unusually quiet and a little sad? ... Subdued.

gre.s: In contrast to his usual exuberance, the comedian seemed oddly ____ throughout the interview, speaking softly and rarely smiling.
gre.clue: speaking softly and rarely smiling

example: After the heavy defeat, the usually noisy bus ride back to Sylhet was subdued, and most players slept or stared out of the windows.

en: Someone or something that takes the place of another
hook: SURROGATE: a SUBSTITUTE who stands in.
story: Surrogate. Someone or something that takes the place of another. When Tasnim's parents went to work in Dubai, her aunt in Rajshahi raised her. She packed her tiffin every morning, went to every parents' meeting, and sat beside her through every fever. On the day Tasnim passed her board exams, it was her aunt she hugged first. For ten years, her aunt had been a surrogate mother. Surrogate comes from the Latin for putting someone in another's place, so think of a substitute. So, what word means someone who stands in for another? ... Surrogate.

gre.s: Unable to attend the ceremony himself, the ailing laureate sent his daughter as a ____ to accept the award and read the speech he had written.
gre.clue: Unable to attend the ceremony himself

example: Keepers at some panda reserves wear panda costumes and act as surrogate mothers for cubs that are being prepared for the wild.

en: Passing quickly, not lasting long
hook: TRANSIENT: in TRANSIT, just passing through.
story: Transient. Passing quickly; not lasting long. When Sabbir failed his first university exam, the pain felt enormous. He skipped dinner and stared at the hostel ceiling all night. A month later he passed the retake, and by the next term he could hardly remember why he had been so upset. The pain had been transient. Like a kalbaishakhi storm in April, it came hard and passed quickly. Transient shares its root with transit: something transient is only passing through. So, what word describes a feeling that does not last long? ... Transient.

gre.s: The economist argued that the price spike was ____, the result of a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change in demand.
gre.clue: a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change

example: The town's population is largely transient, since most residents are construction workers who move on once each project ends.

en: A formal written work dealing systematically with a subject
hook: TREATISE: a book that TREATS a subject thoroughly.
story: Treatise. A formal written work that deals with a subject systematically. Nusrat's grandfather was a soil scientist who spent twenty years writing one book on the rice varieties of Bengal. Chapter by chapter, it covered soil, seasons, history and cooking, every claim carefully argued. When young researchers came to his house to thank him, Nusrat felt a glow of pride. His book was a true treatise. A treatise treats its subject fully; do not confuse it with a treaty, an agreement between nations. So, what word names a formal, systematic book on one subject? ... Treatise.

gre.s: Far from being a casual collection of anecdotes, the book is a rigorous ____, methodically working through every aspect of the philosopher's theory of justice.
gre.clue: methodically working through every aspect

example: In the eleventh century, Ibn Sina wrote a medical treatise so thorough that European universities taught from it for centuries.
